title: Homage to the fever
hookLine: "homage to the cold fever." it sounds like a line for a god. an Atharva Veda hymn says it to a sickness
carry: namah: bow even to the power you fear
tomorrow: a hymn to the healer's own hands
last: MARROW TO MARROW, JOINT TO JOINT.

lines: THE HYMN THAT BOWS TO IT.
cards: Homage to the cold fever. Homage to the burning one. Said aloud, it could be a line from a temple, offered to a god.
It's said to a sickness. Anyone who has sat up at night beside someone burning and shivering may have muttered at the fever itself: go away, leave them alone.
The Atharva Veda has hymns that speak to fever like that, as if it can hear. And one of them, before it asks the fever to leave, bows.

teach.b: The Atharva Veda's word for fever is takman, and in these hymns takman is spoken to like a someone, not a something. One hymn begins by naming where the fever comes from.

teach.h: BORN WHERE FIRE ENTERED THE WATERS.
teach.b: In paraphrase: when fire entered the waters and burned, there, they say, is your birthplace. So the healer starts by knowing the fever's family: it came from fire. Then the hymn names its shapes.
The cold fever. The burning one. The fever that comes back the next day, and the one that comes back on the third.
Then the line from the start of today.

teach.h: HOMAGE TO THE FEVER, THEN: GO.
teach.b: Homage to the cold fever. Homage to the burning one. Namah: the same word people use to bow to a god, said to a sickness.
Why bow first? The hymn doesn't explain. But the habit runs deep in Hinduism.

teach.h: THE RUDRAM: HOMAGE TO RUDRA'S ANGER.
teach.b: The Shri Rudram, one of the most chanted Vedic hymns, opens with homage to Rudra's anger and to his arrow, and then asks him to be kind.
Across north India, many families still honor Sheetala Mata, the cool one, a goddess linked with fevers and pox, praying that she'll be gentle with their children.

teach.h: BOW TO WHAT YOU FEAR. THEN ASK.
teach.b: One reading ties these together: Hindus bow even to the powers they fear. Name them fully, honor their strength, then ask them to pass gently. The bow isn't giving up.
In the fever hymn, the homage comes with the request: leave. So the family at the bedside never pretends the sickness is small, and never stops asking it to go.

how: The Atharva Veda's hymns to takman, fever, address the sickness directly, naming its origin and its forms, offering it homage and asking it to depart; they belong to the Atharva Veda's healing hymns.

games.q: what does “the atharva veda's healing hymns” mean?
o: hymns that blame the sick for their own fever
hymns that praise fever as a gift to be kept
hymns that honor a fever, then ask it to go

games.q: the fever hymn — tap the pairs.
p: fever, spoken to like a someone

s: the fever hymn only curses the fever
it also offers homage: homage to the cold fever, homage to the burning one.
the hymn says the fever's birthplace is where fire entered the waters
the healer starts by naming where the fever came from.
the hymn explains why it bows to the fever
it doesn't say why. readers take it more than one way.

games.q: Sam reads the fever hymn and asks: if you bow to the fever, aren't you just giving in to it?
o: yes: the bow means accepting the sickness
no: honor its strength, then ask it to go, as the hymn does
yes, which is why the hymn never asks it to leave
games.why: Hindus bow even to powers they fear, as the Rudram bows to Rudra's anger. name it, honor it, then ask it to pass gently.

practice: Bring to mind a time you were sick and someone stayed, a parent, a partner, a roommate, a nurse whose name you never learned, and see the room: the cloth, the glass of water, the voice in the dark.
Let thanks rise toward them, whether they're near or far or gone, and if someone you know is sick now, hold them too, the way you were once held. If you pray, pray for them.

wordCard.voice: The Atharva Veda's healing hymns. Takman, fever: named by its birthplace and its shapes, given namah, homage, and asked to go. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the Atharva Veda's word for fever, addressed in its healing hymns.

carryVoice: Your line: namah, bow even to the power you fear. Then ask it to go. Rest well.
